family_judgments.evidence: All formats target an imperative instruction, but the MCQ measures recognition among overtly labeled syntactic alternatives whereas the other formats require production; the productive formats also inherit an unscored phrasal-verb word-order choice.
The formats retain the same declared construct—an English imperative clause. Recognition versus production changes response mechanism and nuisance burden, not the KC definition.
Each item instantiates the same situation: after the cake is removed, Alex directs Sam to switch off the oven.

criteria.evidence: The learner must supply a direct instruction with a bare verb, realizing the declared imperative-clause KC.

Producing the keyed wording also involves the separable phrasal verb “turn off” and its object placement, but these are limited lexical/syntactic burdens rather than a major additional grammatical construct.

“Turn the oven off.” is a linguistically and contextually reasonable imperative using the supplied lexical material; the separable phrasal verb permits both object placements.

summary: The family consistently targets imperative formation, but all free-response versions reject the equally valid separable-phrasal-verb order “Turn the oven off.” This determinacy and accepted-response-coverage defect is blocking.
